report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

info.title: Why and How to Model Trends and Time-Varying Experimental Effects Using Mixed-Effects Models: A Simulation Study and a Tutorial

text.text: Data from repeated-measures experiments (e.g., response time data, electrophysiological data) can show systematic changes in outcomes over time, so-called (temporal) trends.
When analyzing experimental effects between conditions, different trends per condition can cause the experimental effect to vary with time, for example, to decline over the course of the experiment.

Previous research has shown that ignoring time-varying effects in an analysis can influence results and distort conclusions, whereas explicit modeling yields more informative results and valuable insights into the underlying (psychological) processes.

This article provides a systematic introduction to modeling trends and time-varying experimental effects in experimental data, accounting for fixed trends (across participants) as well as random (person-specific individual) trends.

We consider different modeling approaches: exact parametric models, linear or polynomial growth curve models, generalized additive mixed models (GAMMs) and the generalized additive mixed models can effectively detect and model time-varying experimental effects across a range of trend shapes under realistic conditions, provided that the random-effects structure is adequately specified.

• More recently proposed RE-EM trees require larger samples to achieve estimation accuracy and out-of-sample generalizability comparable to those of linear and polynomial growth curve models and generalized additive mixed models.
• Combining the complementary strengths of different methods in terms of flexibility, interpretability, and statistical inference can enhance our understanding of cognitive phenomena.
recently proposed random-effects-expectation-maximization (RE-EM) trees.

We provide an overview of these different modeling approaches and compare their performance and data requirements in two simulation studies based on the characteristics of realistic data from a cognitive response time experiment.
We conclude that polynomial models suffice for simple smooth trends.
Otherwise, GAMMs and RE-EM trees are more suited.

We derive specific recommendations for their application from our results, provide a tutorial on how these models can be applied in the open source software R, and explain how their results can be interpreted along with presenting annotated R-code.
We conclude with a recommended workflow on how a combination of the investigated methods can help researchers better understand time-varying effects.

• Researchers should always consider modeling temporal trends and time-varying effects, as they can inform substantive theories, increase statistical power, and prevent erroneous conclusions due to hidden moderation by time.

In experimental psychology and cognitive neuroscience, it is common to measure outcomes multiple times for each participant (e.g., recording response times, eye tracking data, fMRI or EEG across several trials).
The experimental effects of interest are typically computed as the average differences in these outcomes across experimental conditions.
This procedure is grounded in the notion that averaging across trials can yield more reliable estimates of experimental effects by mitigating unsystematic noise.

However, this approach is based on the assumption that all experimental trials are interchangeable and that the variance in the outcome across trials over time is introduced by nuisance variables alone.

We propose that a different perspective be adopted by considering repeated-measures data as longitudinal data and explicitly examining systematic changes in the outcome over time, referred to as (temporal) trends.

text.text: Previous research has already investigated trends in various outcome measures across different experimental paradigms, demonstrating the potential for longitudinal analyses to uncover meaningful patterns such as habituation or attention processes (e.g., Dignath et al., 2019; Fink et al., 2024; Kalus et al., 2015; Langner et al., 2010; Lorist et al., 2000; McLaughlin et al., 2023; Muller et al., 2013; Pattyn et al., 2008; Van Rij et al., 2019; Volkmer et al., 2022; Von Gunten et al., 2018; Wetzel et al., 2021).

text.text: In longitudinal data with trends, the outcome value systematically depends on the specific time point of its observation, making the temporal order of the observations non-ignorable.
In designs with multiple experimental conditions, there may even be different trends for each condition.

Consequently, the difference in outcomes across these conditions (i.e., the experimental effect) should also be considered conditional on a specific time point, thus leading to a time-varying experimental effect, which occurs when different trends per condition lead to the experimental effects changing over time.

This point is crucial because time-varying experimental effects can no longer be adequately described by the so-called marginal experimental effect, which is the average experimental effect across time points. 1 Consequently, these marginal experimental effects can no longer be meaningfully compared between studies of different durations (for a discussion see e.g., McLaughlin et al., 2023; Volkmer et al., 2022; Widmann et al., 2025). Volkmer et al. (2022) provided a specific example of this phenomenon in their analysis of data from an auditory-visual distraction experiment (i.e., an oddball paradigm).

text.text: In this experiment, each trial required a forced-choice response to a visual stimulus, which was preceded by either a frequently occurring standard sound or a randomly interspersed distractor sound.
Participants exhibited slower responses in trials following distractor sounds versus standard sounds, a phenomenon commonly referred to as the distraction effect.
Crucially, the distraction effect decreased over time due to different trends in response times (RTs) for each condition (Volkmer et al., 2022; Wetzel et al., 2021).

Several different mixed-effects models can be used to model trends per condition, allowing researchers to make their choice on the basis of their prior knowledge and desired flexibility: 1.
Exact parametric mixed-effects models can be used when the exact shape of the trend per condition can be mathematically specified a priori.
Linear and polynomial growth curve models can be used to approximate various simpler smooth trends.
Generalized additive mixed models can be used to model nonlinear trends, even without any prior knowledge about the shape.

This paper consists of three parts: First, we introduce the basic concepts of these models to ensure that readers who are familiar with linear mixed-effects models can follow along.
Next, we report two simulation studies in which we investigated the performance of these models in several realistic scenarios.
This approach allowed us to explore each model's data requirements and performance.
To our knowledge, no systematic comparison of these models has been conducted before.
Finally, we illustrate the implementation and interpretation of all these models in a tutorial using a real data example with annotated R-code.
We conclude with a recommended workflow for analyzing time-varying experimental effects.
For readers only interested in applying these models to their data, we recommend focusing on the introduction and tutorial part.
Mixed-effects models (MEMs, also known as hierarchical models, multilevel models, and random coefficients models) are widely used to analyze data from repeated-measures designs.

We assume that the reader is familiar with the basics of these models, and we only briefly reiterate the basic notation to enable a better understanding of the trend models (for a detailed introduction tailored to experimental psychology, see e.g., Bagiella et al., 2000; Maxwell et al., 2018).

In the following sections, we explain how this model can be expanded to account for trends.

For the sake of accessibility, we limit our introduction to different approaches for investigating trends in a design featuring two experimental conditions, with random intercepts and random slopes for the experimental condition.
Furthermore, we first focus on situations where trends per condition are identical across participants (fixed trends).

The basic idea behind all the following approaches is that they include time (e.g., in the form of the trial number as in our example, but other metrics are possible) as a predictor variable so that: where f (condition it , time it ) denotes the model-specific estimation of the trend per condition (i.e., an interaction term in a broader sense).
Wheras exact parametric models are based on the assumption that the exact form of the trend is known, the other modeling options approximate the trend on a data-driven basis.

Sometimes, theory predicts a very specific trend (e.g., the Ebbinghaus forgetting curve, Ebbinghaus, 1913), which can be directly specified as a (non)linear MEM by using either a transformed time variable (e.g., the log of the trial number, number of experimental blocks) or by specifying a particular (nonlinear, e.g., sine, exponential) function (Lindstrom & Bates, 1990; Pinheiro & Bates, 2000).

text.text: However, these models impose a strict assumption on the shape of the trend, making it difficult to detect unexpected or deviating shapes.
At worst, true trends may be obscured by the specified shape, resulting in a false sense of confidence in the model's parameters and potentially false conclusions.
The same problem arises with nonlinear transformations of the time metric.
Additionally, nonlinear MEMs featuring functions such as exponentials or sines are notoriously difficult to estimate (e.g., McCormick, 2023).

text.text: Given these disadvantages, we recommend that explicit parametric models should be used only when a specific functional form of the trends is expected.
Otherwise, we think the following approximate models are more preferable.

MEMs that model linear (first degree polynomial) or higher-order polynomial growth over time (trends) are referred to as linear or polynomial growth curve models (GCMs) (for an introduction see also Kristjansson et al., 2007; Mirman, 2017).

text.text: Linear GCMs are appealing because they are parsimonious and their parameters have a straightforward interpretation that follows the principles of regression analysis.
For quadratic, cubic, or even higher order GCMs, the interpretation becomes less intuitive because the number of parameters increases rapidly with the order of the polynomial.
Additionally, the parameters do not intuitively translate into the shape of the curve.
For instance, a significant quadratic term does not necessarily indicate a U-shape over the observed time range (Simonsohn, 2018).

Additionally, all fixed coefficients in GCMs can also be added as random coefficients.
GCMs can easily be extended by incorporating random coefficients for the linear or polynomial interaction, thus allowing trends to vary by condition and individual (random trends).
The challenge with polynomial GCMs lies in determining the appropriate degree.

Higher order polynomials tend to fit the data too closely (overfitting), resulting in overly complex ("wiggly") trends (e.g., Runge's phenomenon, an "artificial wiggliness" at the margins of the data or time range, Runge, 1901).

text.text: Mixed-effects splines, more frequently known as Generalized Additive Mixed Models (GAMMs; Baayen & Linke, 2020; Hastie et al., 2009; Wood, 2017), are a semi-parametric approach for modeling smooth relationships of arbitrary shapes (that might occur in psychophysiological data) and can be applied to repeated-measures data (see also Van Rij et al., 2019, for an extensive tutorial).

text.text: GAMMs allow for very flexible approximations by using splines to model trends per condition.
The general idea of splines is to combine simple functions into a flexible curve that can approximate complex trends without specifying their exact overall shape in advance.

Because this shape emerges from the combined contributions of these functions, individual coefficients generally do not have a straightforward substantive interpretation in terms of the overall trend.
Consequently, the fitted trends are typically inspected graphically to understand their shapes.

text.text: The B-spline is easiest to understand in the piecewise-linear example (see (cubic splines), a penalization is introduced by adding a cost for curvature.
This way, the fit to the data is maximized while simultaneously constraining the curvature.
The basic principle of the penalization can be understood with a minimal squared residuals example: model fit = sum of squared residuals + λ • curvature penalty.
One very commonly applied penalty accumulates the squared second derivative across the observed time range.
Recall that the second derivative describes how rapidly a curve's slope changes.
Therefore, a straight line receives no curvature penalty because its slope does not change, whereas pronounced bends increase the penalty.
The smoothing parameter λ determines how strongly the penalty affects the estimation.
Larger values force less curved fits because an additional bend must improve the fit enough to justify its additional penalty.
The basis functions and knot positions remain unchanged; the model just penalizes the spline coefficients.
In (penalized) GAMMs, the flexibility of a spline is governed by two main hyperparameters: the smoothing parameter λ and the basis dimension.

Whereas λ is typically optimized automatically during model fitting, researchers specify the basis dimension and should check whether increasing it allows a substantially better fit to the data (Wood, 2017, see also the tutorial section).
To sum up, splines can flexibly approximate trends of arbitrary shape with minimal prior knowledge.

Their flexibility (over-and underfitting) is governed both by the hyperparameters (basis dimension and by the smoothing penalty), so these choices and the adequacy of the resulting fit need to be considered.
However, splines alone can not yet account for the multilevel structure of repeated-measures data.

text.text: The challenge in fitting splines lies partly in avoiding over-or underfitting, that is, choosing settings that allow enough flexibility without fitting noise.
If the basis dimension is too small or the smoothing penalty too strong, the curve may miss real changes in the data.
Conversely, a very large basis dimension combined with too little smoothing can fit random fluctuations and produce an overly wiggly curve.

Thus, although smoothing parameters are often estimated automatically, the basis dimension and the adequacy of the resulting fit still require consideration; model diagnostics and sensitivity to reasonable alternative settings can help assess these choices (Wood, 2017).

text.text: As with higher-order polynomials, spline flexibility also increases model complexity and can require more data and computation.
The resulting model can therefore be harder to summarize and compare, even though plots make the fitted trends accessible.
As explained above, the estimated spline parameters can not be interpreted directly.
Instead, researchers typically rely on visual inspection to gain an understanding of the trend per condition.
This issue becomes even more problematic when individual trends per condition are allowed, resulting in one graph per condition and participant.
However, the parametric fixed and random effects have a clear interpretation (see tutorial section).

text.text: In the following, we briefly explain the general idea behind RE-EM trees (see Strobl et al., 2009, for a more in-depth technical introduction to tree-algorithms).

text.text: RE-EM trees may be conceived of as MEMs in which the fixed-effects part is replaced by a regression tree, which partitions (splits) the data into segments called nodes on the basis of the predictor variables (Breiman et al., 1984).
text.formatted: RE-EM trees may be conceived of as MEMs in which the fixed-effects part is replaced by a regression tree, which partitions (splits) the data into segments called nodes on the basis of the predictor variables <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Breiman et al., 1984)</ref>.

text.text: The estimated value is usually the mean outcome across all observations in this node and identical for all observations in each node (the median or other sample statistics are also possible).
In contrast to splines, split points may occur on any of the predictor variables (e.g., experimental conditions, time, other potential covariates).
The splitting is done recursively and is entirely data-driven.

text.text: One prominent approach is to choose the splitting variable and split point such that the sum of squared errors is minimized within each node (i.e., the squared difference between estimated and observed outcome values).
This approach is known as the classification and regression tree (CART; Breiman et al., 1984) algorithm.
text.formatted: This approach is known as the classification and regression tree (CART; <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Breiman et al., 1984)</ref> algorithm.

text.text: When applying regression trees, it is crucial to control the tree complexity to avoid overfitting (Breiman et al., 1984).
text.formatted: When applying regression trees, it is crucial to control the tree complexity to avoid overfitting <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Breiman et al., 1984)</ref>.

text.text: Otherwise, CART trees would grow until each observation ends up in its own node, which is undesirable because the results would not generalize beyond the current data set.
Stopping rules and pruning are two methods used to achieve this objective (Breiman et al., 1984).
text.formatted: Stopping rules and pruning are two methods used to achieve this objective <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Breiman et al., 1984)</ref>.

text.text: They operate at different stages of the tree-building process.
Stopping rules are criteria set during the tree-growing process to decide when to stop splitting (hyperparameters).

Common stopping criteria include requiring a minimum number of observations in each node or specifying a complexity parameter that determines the minimum amount that the total explained variance must increase in order for a split to be made (Sela & Simonoff, 2012).
text.formatted: Common stopping criteria include requiring a minimum number of observations in each node or specifying a complexity parameter that determines the minimum amount that the total explained variance must increase in order for a split to be made <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">(Sela & Simonoff, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Pruning, on the other hand, is applied after the tree has been fully grown and involves removing some of the splits to simplify the tree and improve its generalizability.
Typically, cross-validation is used to decide how much a tree must be pruned (Sela & Simonoff, 2012).
text.formatted: Typically, cross-validation is used to decide how much a tree must be pruned <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">(Sela & Simonoff, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Cross-validation is a technique for estimating how well models fit on new data (estimating generalizability).

The observations in the dataset are randomly split into subsets where a model (here a tree with a certain number of splits corresponding to a certain complexity parameter) is estimated on one subset and used to predict outcomes from a different subset.

This process is typically repeated 10 times (widely used default in machine learning, balancing estimation accuracy and computational cost; e.g., Hastie et al., 2009), and the resulting prediction errors are combined into a cross-validation error.
text.formatted: This process is typically repeated 10 times (widely used default in machine learning, balancing estimation accuracy and computational cost; e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Hastie et al., 2009)</ref>, and the resulting prediction errors are combined into a cross-validation error.

text.text: By choosing the complexity parameter value that minimizes the cross-validation error, a better balance between model fit and model complexity can be achieved (Breiman et al., 1984).
text.formatted: By choosing the complexity parameter value that minimizes the cross-validation error, a better balance between model fit and model complexity can be achieved <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Breiman et al., 1984)</ref>.

text.text: Pruning based on cross-validation is less dependent on arbitrary decisions by researchers compared with implementing a stopping criterion.
We explain in more detail how the complexity of the trees can be controlled in practice in the tutorial section.
The tree algorithm described so far can be applied to independent observations only.
RE-EM trees therefore combine regression trees with random effects to allow the trees to be fit to repeated-measures data (Sela & Simonoff, 2012).

text.text: The primary advantage of the RE-EM tree lies in its ability to include any number of fixed-effect predictors and (nonlinear) interactions while still providing a systematic way to understand its splitting rules.

This approach could be particularly beneficial for designs with multiple dichotomous predictor variables, such as experimental conditions, where the tree can be used to determine which (combinations of) conditions have different trends (variable selection).
Similar to GAMMs, RE-EM trees can be used without any prior knowledge about the shape of the trend, as they can approximate any smooth function using a step-function.
The step-function approximation can be used to infer smooth shapes (see also simulation and tutorial section).
Moreover, they can also approximate non-smooth functions, such as when a sudden change in the outcome is expected, but the time point is unknown.
Still, it has been shown that regression trees are worse at approximating (quasi-)linear functions than nonlinear functions (Gottard et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Still, it has been shown that regression trees are worse at approximating (quasi-)linear functions than nonlinear functions <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Gottard et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: However, the flexibility of RE-EM trees relies on selection of stopping criteria and is limited to the tree part (fixed effects) of RE-EM trees.
Random effects, such as individual differences in trends, can (so far) only be specified using parametric functions (Sela & Simonoff, 2012).
text.formatted: Random effects, such as individual differences in trends, can (so far) only be specified using parametric functions <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">(Sela & Simonoff, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, CART algorithms have a tendency to select variables that offer many splitting points, resulting in a bias toward including continuous or polytomous predictors over dichotomous ones.
There are alternative algorithms that adopt different splitting criteria to avoid this bias (Fu & Simonoff, 2015; Hothorn et al., 2006).
text.formatted: There are alternative algorithms that adopt different splitting criteria to avoid this bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Fu & Simonoff, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Hothorn et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, unlike the previously explained approaches, RE-EM trees do not provide any formal inferential statistics, such as significance tests or confidence intervals.
This omission is especially detrimental because trees are often unstable, and results depend heavily on the specific sample.
Split points and selected variables can differ tremendously across samples, but this uncertainty is not apparent in the model output.

However, there are approaches for mitigating this problem such as conditional inference trees (Hothorn et al., 2006), stable trees (Michel et al., 2016), or random forests (see Capitaine et al., 2021; Hajjem et al., 2014, for an implementation for longitudinal data).
text.formatted: However, there are approaches for mitigating this problem such as conditional inference trees <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Hothorn et al., 2006)</ref>, stable trees <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Michel et al., 2016)</ref>, or random forests (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Capitaine et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Hajjem et al., 2014</ref>, for an implementation for longitudinal data).

text.text: All the methods described above are theoretically capable of modeling time-varying effects.
We expect simplistic linear GCMs to underfit non-linear trend shapes, whereas higher-order GCMs are at risk of overfitting simpler trends.
GAMMs and RE-EM trees are suited to recover various shapes of trends (non-linear, RE-EM tree also stepwise), but their performance is known to depend on the settings of the hyperparameters.

Given that data from psychological experiments are notoriously noisy at the trial level, it is important to assess whether these methods can recover (nonlinear) trends in experimental data under realistic scenarios.
Additionally, we are not aware of any applications of tree-based methods to experimental data in psychology, and it remains to be seen if these methods can be useful in this context.
To obtain initial evidence on these questions, we conducted two monte carlo simulations to derive practical guidelines for researchers who want to apply these methods.

In a first simulation, we investigated the models' abilities to recover trends and detect experimental effects under various realistic data situations and shapes of fixed trends, that is, under the restriction that all participants share the same trend per condition.
In a second simulation, we investigated scenarios with random trends, that is, with realistic inter-individual variability in the temporal trends per condition.

text.text: Model performance out of sample is a key metric for model evaluation, as researchers want to generalize their results to a population.

We simulated one large test data set with N = 10000 for each simulation scenario to predict the RT for this test data set with each models fixed effects as a marker for generalizability of the fixed effects to new data from new participants.
Similar to the GOF in sample we calculated a GOF out of sample , with test dataset RT and estimated ˆ︃ RT based on the models' fixed effects.
We investigated potential bias in the estimation of the random-effects parameters, specifically, the standard deviations of random intercepts and slopes, as well as their correlation.
We also examined how often models detected a difference in trends between sound types.

For GCMs and GAMMs, we used the number of significant model comparisons between models with the same trend for both sound types versus models that allowed for different trends per sound type (i.e. power or false positive rate -FPR -of the time-varying experimental effect).
For RE-EM trees, there is no statistical significance test for the time-varying effect.
Instead, we counted the number of trees containing a split for both sound type and trial number as a measure of detection rate.
We also investigated the number of splits and splitting variables conducted to further assess the fitting behavior of RE-EM trees.
Simulation results can be reproduced using the code available on GitHub.
Linear and polynomial GCMs, GAMMs, and RE-EM trees consistently achieved convergence in nearly 100% of the runs.
Runs with non-converged benchmark (i.e., data-generating exact-parametric) models (0.38%), linear GCMs (0.005%) and polynomial GCMs (0.002%) were excluded.
In addition, we observed occasional anomalous solutions for the benchmark model in rare cases.
These were characterized by implausibly extreme values of the trend parameters and therefore could not be considered valid benchmarks.

Thus, we applied a robust outlier criterion and removed another 0.13% of the remaining samples because the benchmark models yielded a fixed-effects-based R² more than 3.5 median absolute deviations away from the median of their respective scenario (Wilcox, 2012, p. 86).

text.text: All models showed sufficient detection of the time-varying effect when a trend was present in the data generating model.
The differential trends between conditions were detected in 98.17% to 100% of the samples across scenarios with time-varying effects.

Only two exceptions to this pattern occurred, both in "limited data" scenarios (i.e., conditions with high residual variance, small sample size N = 50, and low sampling frequency T = 90): First, for exponential trends, the time-varying effect was detected in only 86.41% of the samples by linear GCMs, 85.08% for GAMMs, 89.83% for polynomial GCMs, and 74.36% for RE-EM trees.
Second, RE-EM trees had greater difficulty in detecting linear trends (90.00%).
Notably, the RE-EM tree was still able to reliably detect the marginal experimental effect (with 95.60% detection rate) even when the underlying time-varying effect was not detected.
The FPR for the time-varying effect (in the control scenarios) for GCMs and RE-EM trees ranged from 2.2% to 6.2% and thus did not deviate to a notable extend from the nominal 5%.
GAMMs tended to be more conservative (1.1% to 2.8%).

Overall, polynomial GCMs, GAMMs, and RE-EM trees were all effective in detecting and estimating various (fixed) time-varying effects in sample under various realistic conditions for noisy measures such as RT, while also accurately estimating random intercepts and slopes for the experimental condition.

Notably, all models demonstrated sensitivity to the time-varying effect of almost 100%, under most realistic scenarios-featuring 50 participants, 90 trials (whereof only 18 interspersed distractor trials showed a trend, so the decisive number of trials per experimental condition was 18), random slopes for the experimental condition and skewed residuals with realistic RT variance.
The only notable drop in detection rate for the time-varying effect occurred in the limited data scenarios (N = 50, T = 90, high residual variance SD = 108), particularly for the exponential trend.

This provides an orientation for minimal data requirements for research involving very noisy data with few participants and numbers of observations, as is often the case in research on RT in young children for example.
To further examine minimal data requirements, we reran the simulation with N = 20, T = 90 and high residual variance.
We replicated the same pattern in model performance, but with lower detection rates (down to a minimum of 39% in the exponential scenario but still > 97% for the stepwise scenario).

text.text: Additionally, we found a larger number of non-converging models for the benchmark (nlme) models (up to 25% in the exponential trend scenario) and GAMMs (up to 15 -18% for all trend scenarios).
Taken together, we encourage researchers to gain practical experience on detection and convergence in their data.
For studies with (very) small sample sizes, we recommend pooling data from similar experiments together to achieve a larger sample size for analysis.
Differences between models mainly emerged regarding the out-of-sample generalizability, that is necessary in order to draw valid conclusions about the underlying population.
Unsurprisingly, the linear GCM performed well only for linear or absent trends.
A strict linear model is inherently unable to represent any strong nonlinearity, especially non-monotonous shapes (see Figure 7, upper row) and always underfits in these scenarios.

text.text: In contrast, the 3 rd -degree-polynomial GCM performed much better, providing reasonable approximations and good generalizability for all smooth trends.
Notably, in scenarios with a (quasi-)linear trend, small sample size, and small number of trials, the polynomial GCM tended to overfit a little, resulting in a "wiggly" appearance.
This result occured because the polynomial model, while subsuming linear trends as a special case, still retains higher order terms that in practice do not equal exactly zero in smaller samples.

This overfitting tendency decreased with larger samples, leaving only minor artifacts at the edges of the time range due to the mathematical limitations of the 3 rd -degree-polynomial (e.g., two turning points).
For the stepwise trend, approximation by 3 rd -degree-polynomials proved too coarse.

However, this issue could be addressed by employing a higher order polynomial (e.g., 7 th degree) which achieves approximations comparable to GAMMs, but also suffers from Runge's Phenomenon (Runge, 1901).
text.formatted: However, this issue could be addressed by employing a higher order polynomial (e.g., 7 th degree) which achieves approximations comparable to GAMMs, but also suffers from Runge's Phenomenon <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Runge, 1901)</ref>.

text.text: Overall, our results emphasize that lower order polynomial GCMs are effective for modeling various trends if a polynomial of sufficient degree is used.
The primary challenge with GCMs lies in determining a reasonable degree to avoid under-or overfitting and still maintain interpretability (see Tutorial section).
GAMMs adequately approximated all smooth trends and also managed to approximate the stepwise trend.
However, some systematic "wiggle" artifacts emerged preceding and following the sudden change.

These artifacts can be explained when considering splines as filters (Kauermann et al., 2011): The stepwise trend resembles a step function, and it has been established that filters produce characteristic artifacts when encountering discontinuities (e.g., Widmann et al., 2015).

text.text: Thus, the GAMM pattern observed for the stepwise trend resembles typical step responses of filters.
Regarding the FPR, we observed a surprisingly low FPR for GAMMs compared with the other models (around 1.1 to 2.8% vs the nominal 5%).

The model comparison we used for inference of the time-varying effect is recommended for being the least liberal option (Sóskuthy, 2017), but this very low false-positive rate should be investigated in future research.

text.text: Overall, in line with previous research, GAMMs proved to be a flexible and well-performing option for modeling trends (Sóskuthy, 2017; Van Rij et al., 2019).

text.text: RE-EM trees also achieved good approximations with high generalizability, even for smooth trends, when sample sizes were sufficiently large in terms of participants and trials, performing surprisingly well on average despite their reputation for limited effectiveness in modeling continuous functions (Gottard et al., 2022).

text.text: Nonetheless, in scenarios with small numbers of participants and trials, RE-EM trees performed worse in terms of generalization of smooth trends and detecting differences in (quasi-) linear trends scenarios compared to the other methods.
For stepwise trends, RE-EM trees outperformed GAMMs and GCMs as expected.
Most notably, the estimated stepwise shapes from RE-EM trees were fundamentally different from the smooth shapes estimated by the other models across all scenarios.
In this simulation, we know the underlying true shape, whereas in real world applications, we do not.
It is a substantive question to determine which shape best resembles the underlying processes.

Abrupt changes may occur, for instance, when participants change their response strategy (Ollman, 1977), learn a new concept or rule (e.g., in the wisconsin card sorting test, Dehaene & Changeux, 1991) or in the context of bistable perception effects (Blake & Logothetis, 2002), where qualitative changes in stimuli perception may happen at certain points in the experiment.

text.text: Nonetheless, our results demonstrate that it is possible to infer a smooth shape from a sufficiently detailed stepwise shape (e.g., a sine from a tree with seven final nodes, as shown in Figure 7), and vice versa (e.g., the GAMMs' smooth approximation of the stepwise trend in Figure 7).

text.text: Overall, RE-EM trees proved to be quite flexible across different trend shapes but provided no advantage over (correctly specified) exact parametric models, polynomial GCMs or GAMMs for smooth shapes.
However, they require larger numbers of participants and trials than the other models to avoid overly simplistic fits (e.g., only one or two splits) and adequately represent smooth trends.

When investigating the number of tree splits we also witnessed the instability of the CART algorithm (e.g., Hothorn et al., 2006; Strobl et al., 2009), leading to larger variability in GOF across samples compared to the other models.

text.text: While the uncertainty of the other MEMs is reflected in the provided standard errors, the instability and (increased) uncertainty of the RE-EM tree is not apparent by looking at only one sample.
The practical implications are discussed in the tutorial section.

We derived our simulation scenarios from a real data set to maximize ecological validity and designed simulation scenarios that are challenging for the models (e.g., noisier data than RT, various nonlinear trends).

Consequently, the results clearly demonstrate that the proposed models can be effectively applied to data sets from experiments that are sufficiently similar to this relatively simple design even with noisy measures such as RT.

We think the recommendations derived from the simulation study can be confidently generalized to experimental data with a minimum of 18 trials per experimental condition and participant (with more trials recommended for the RE-EM tree), randomization on the trial level (no block-wise randomization), similarly or less noisy, skewed measures, and experimental data with unbalanced experimental conditions (e.g. 20% vs 80% of trials).
As with any other experiment, the generalizability of monte carlo simulations depends on specific design choices.
In the following, we want to reflect critically on some of our choices and their potential impact on the generalizability of our results: 1.
Most importantly, we assumed fixed trends, that is, one trend per condition with a fixed shape across participants.
This assumption may be realistic for very common phenomena (e.g., habituation of pupil dilation, Fink et al., 2024), but individual trends per participant may occur for a lot of real processes.
text.formatted: This assumption may be realistic for very common phenomena (e.g., habituation of pupil dilation, <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Fink et al., 2024)</ref>, but individual trends per participant may occur for a lot of real processes.

text.text: To address this, we conducted another simulation investigating model performance under participant-specific trends for each condition (see next section).
We also discuss possible modeling options for random trends in the tutorial section.
Related to the first point, for all models, we assumed that the correct random effects structure was specified.
It remains an open question how well the models perform when the random-effects structure is misspecified (see next section).
More complex experimental designs with multiple experimental conditions are quite common.
However, as long as the number of trials per condition is sufficiently large, increased complexity should not per se have an impact on the models' performances.
Options to handle more complex experimental designs are discussed in the tutorial section.

The simulation results for GAMMs and RE-EM trees depend on a careful selection of their hyperparameters (i.e., amount of penalization, stopping criteria, and pruning), which were tailored for this specific, yet realistic, experimental data context.
For GAMMs, these choices typically have very limited influence on estimation (Perperoglou et al., 2019).
text.formatted: For GAMMs, these choices typically have very limited influence on estimation <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Perperoglou et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: By contrast, for RE-EM trees, we also ran the simulation with default pruning settings (pruning via one standard error, complexity parameter = 0.001), which resulted in overly simplistic trees with a very small number of splits. 9 We provide more information and recommendations regarding optimal choices for hyperparameters in the tutorial section.

This means their FPR depends on the hyperparameters but can not be specified explicitly.
Conditional inference trees (RE-EM ctrees, Fu & Simonoff, 2015) may be a suitable alternative that circumvents this limitation.

text.text: Additionally, CART trees tend to select continuous over dichotomous predictors (Fu & Simonoff, 2015).

Although we did not observe such problems in this simulation, we acknowledge that more methodological research on mixed-effects trees is needed.
Their use in any research project should be accompanied by appropriate critical reflection.
The results cannot be generalized to very different trend shapes (e.g., rapid oscillation) or changes in effects across trial sequences instead of the whole experiment.
For these scenarios, other models may be more suited (e.g., Keintzel et al., 2026).

text.text: In the previous simulation, our data generating model contained fixed trends and time-varying effects.

However, individuals varying in their individual change in RT over time, or even random interactions between trends and experimental condition are plausible in a lot of processes (Bolger et al., 2019).
text.formatted: However, individuals varying in their individual change in RT over time, or even random interactions between trends and experimental condition are plausible in a lot of processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Bolger et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Random trends should be considered in the modeling process for two reasons:

First of all, individual differences in trends may provide interesting insights into the substantive phenomena (e.g., Bolger et al., 2019; Elbe et al., 2024; Sörqvist et al., 2012) and could also take on various (nonlinear) shapes.

Second, unmodeled random effects introduce heterogeneity into the model and thus may result in false conclusions due to distorted standard error estimates for the fixed effects (e.g., Barr et al., 2013).

The impact of misspecified random trends structure is already visible in this simplistic scenario and can be generalized to more complex models, while maintaining a reasonable runtime for the simulation.

We used the data generating model from the previous simulation and extended it by adding random trends per condition, implemented as random slopes for trial number and a random interaction term between experimental effect and trial number.
The random-effects matrix was again derived from a real data example (Bonmassar et al., 2023).

Both trend scenarios included the random effects as described above, including random trends.

text.text: For model fitting, we centered and rescaled the time variable (trial number) to a range of -2 to 2 to get similar scale for all predictors.
A larger range resulted in much more ill convergence due to large eigen values, whereas smaller ranges resulted in singular fit warnings due to numeric issues with small random effects variances.
For each sample, we fit the same fixed-trends linear and polynomial GCMs, GAMMs and RE-EM trees as before (that is, only including random intercept and slope for sound type, no random trends).
Additionally, we fit a linear GCM with an additional random effect for the time variable, but no random interaction term (random-marginal-trend model) 12 .
We used a linear GCM with correctly specified random effects (including random effect for the time variable and interaction with sound type) as benchmark (random-conditional-trends model).
We used the same dependent measures for model fit, generalizability and recovery of random effects as before.
Misspecified random-effects structures are known to impact FPRs (Barr et al., 2013).

text.text: Therefore, we additionally examined FPRs for the fixed effect of sound type, for the fixed trend in the standard trials and for the fixed difference in trends between conditions (i.e., time-varying effect).
The FPR for sound type was determined using the test of the respective regression coefficient for GCMs and GAMMs.
For RE-EM trees, we determined the number of trees that split once, with sound type as the splitting variable as an FPR proxy.
The FPR for the detection of a trend in standard trials was determined using the test of the regression coefficient of trial number for linear GCMs.
For polynomial GCMs, we conducted a model comparison against a model the trend in the standard trials fixed to zero.
For GAMMs we used the test of the approximate significance of the smooth term in the standard sound type condition.
For RE-EM trees, there is no straightforward way to determine if a trend in standard trials was detected.
Therefore we used the number of trees that only split once and the splitting variable was trial number as a proxy.
The FPR for the time-varying effect was determined as in the fixed-trends simulation for all models.
Fixed-trends linear GCMs, polynomial GCMs, GAMMs, and RE-EM trees always converged.

Runs with non-converged random-conditional-trends linear GCMs (i.e., with both random trend and interaction = benchmark model; 0.23%) or Random-marginal-trends linear GCMs (without random interaction; 0.08%) were excluded.
Most convergence issues were mitigated by centering and rescaling the time variable (see tutorial section for recommendations).
Additionally, we registered a large number of singular fit warnings for random-conditional-trends linear GCMs.

In small N small T conditions, 1.4% of runs yielded singular fits for fixed-trends linear and polynomial GCMs, 0.7% for random-marginal-trend linear GCMs and 58% for random-conditional-trends linear GCMs.

Further examination of the random-effects distributions indicated that a primary source of singularity lay in the random-effects correlations, specifically the correlations between the random interaction term and random slope for sound type, and between the random interaction term and the random slope for the time variable.

text.text: We showed even in a simplistic scenario, the choice of random effects, especially random trends, substantially influences the conclusions drawn from the model results for GCMs, GAMMs and RE-EM trees.

Replicating previous research, we found that unmodeled random effects do not change fixed-effects model fit, but increase FPR due to underestimated standard errors (Barr et al., 2013; Matuschek et al., 2017).

For RE-EM trees, we also observed an especially increased FPR for continuous predictors (time variable), reflecting a known bias of the CART algorithm regarding selection of continuous over dichotomous predictors as splitting variables.

Additionally, we observed that random effects structures including random interaction terms resulted in more singular fit warnings in lme4, that is, estimated variance-covariance matrices with (almost) less than full rank indicating a certain "redundancy" in the random-effects covariances (see the tutorial section for more details).

Overall, the results of our random-trends simulation underline that correct specification of the random effects is mandatory for adequate statistical inference even when the variance of the neglected random slopes may seem negligibly small in absolute values.

When implementing MEMs, researchers are often confronted with convergence issues, that is, the estimation algorithm not arriving at a solution, returning no estimates (or estimates that should not be interpreted).
Depending on the model and software, different strategies can be used to improve model convergence.
First of all, centering variables can be useful.
In our case, we created a centered time variable so that 0 refers to a time point in the middle of the experiment (trial 120).
Secondly, it proved to be useful to rescale the time variable to not range from -119 to 120 but from -2 to 2 (time_scaled).
This way, all predictor variables had a similar range, helping with convergence.
Note that the rescaling influences parameter interpretation, as we will outline below.
Furthermore, different estimation methods are differentially susceptible to convergence issues.
We found GCMs to converge better with REML instead of ML estimation.
Bayesian estimation has also been proposed to circumvent convergence (and singularity) issues (e.g., Bürkner, 2018). 14 Lastly, various model options can be changed.

All packages used in this tutorial also allow custom starting values for the algorithm, which can be helpful.
These values may be taken from descriptive statistics or simpler models.

Another frequent issue encountered by researchers is singularity, that is, estimated variance-covariance matrices with less than full rank indicating a certain "redundancy" in the random-effects covariances.
The source of the singularity can be hard to detect with more than one random slope.
Singular models provide a mathematically correct estimation, but have been argued to have poor power (Matuschek et al., 2017) and some inferential tests may be inappropriate (Bates et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Singular models provide a mathematically correct estimation, but have been argued to have poor power <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Matuschek et al., 2017)</ref> and some inferential tests may be inappropriate <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bates et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Although we found no evidence of these issues in our simulation study, we emphasize that further research is needed to fully understand the impact of singular fits.
There is no straightforward recommendation for handling singular fits in general and how to interpret the random-effects estimates in these models.
Based on our simulation for random trends, we suggest that (nearly) singular random-effects covariance matrices should be accepted if the focus is on interpreting the fixed effects.

text.text: Whenever the specified random-effects structure is less complex than the fixed-effects structure (e.g., some fixed effects have no corresponding random effects), the respective random effects variances have a marginal interpretation.
This becomes clearer when recognizing that random effects are added on top of the fixed effects.

For instance, if the random slope for time and the random interaction term were omitted, the random intercept variance would quantify the variability in participants' marginal RTs in standard trials "averaged" across all trials and the random slope variance for sound type would quantify the variability in participants' marginal distraction effects "averaged" across all trials.

text.text: The raw = TRUE argument inside poly() calculates raw polynomial parameters (e.g., a • x + b • x 2 + c • x 3 ) instead of orthogonal polynomials (software default).

Although orthogonal polynomials provide more stable estimations for higher order polynomials, their parameters are not directly interpretable, so for the sake of this tutorial, we opted for raw polynomials.
The number 3 inside poly() indicates the degree of the polynomial (here: cubic).
Each degree adds two parameters (one per sound type because of the interaction).
Therefore, more observations are required for stable estimation of higher order polynomials.
This poly() syntax is repeated for the random effects in brackets, to fit person-specific polynomial trends per condition.
Given our simulation results, we recommend to choose a random effects structure at least as complex as the fixed effect structure.
Fitting different polynomial degrees per sound type is also possible by using specific :-syntax instead of * (see code on GitHub).

text.text: As in the linear GCM, the fixed intercept represents the estimated RT in standard trials in the middle of the experiment and fixed effect of sound type represents the conditional experimental effect in the middle of the experiment.

However, the estimates for the fixed slope for sound type (9 ms) differs from that in the linear GCM (16 ms; also visible by comparing distance between the dark and light blue lines in trial number 120 in Figures 8 and 9).

text.text: This difference occurred because the polynomial trend more effectively captured the nonlinear shape and thus also the smaller conditional experimental effects in the middle of the experiment.

Here, estimating a linear trend leads to overestimation of the conditional experimental effect in the middle of the experiment, highlighting the importance of modeling nonlinear trends with adequate models.
In this polynomial GCM, the trend per sound type is described by six parameters instead of two.

The three fixed-effects parameters poly(time, 3, raw = T)1 to 3 in Figure 9 describe the polynomial trend in standard trials (i.e., when sound type equals zero) and describe the linear, quadratic, and cubic term, respectively.

text.text: The interaction terms with sound type correspond to the differences in these parameters between sound types.
Thus, the polynomial trend in distractor trials is calculated by adding the respective interaction term parameters soundType:poly(time, 3, raw = T)1 to 3 to the standard trial parameters.

Although specific parameter interpretations can be derived analytically from the polynomial functions, they do not intuitively correspond to the trend's shape (Simonsohn, 2018) and should instead be interpreted as part of the whole equation (Humberg et al., 2019).

text.text: We will discuss this decision below.
The following arguments address the stopping criteria and pruning.

The stopping criteria are set using tree.control, where we set the complexity parameter to cp = 0.0001, allowing splits that contribute only 0.01% of total explained variance (i.e., an increment in R² of only 0.0001; Therneau & Atkinson, 2022).
text.formatted: The stopping criteria are set using tree.control, where we set the complexity parameter to cp = 0.0001, allowing splits that contribute only 0.01% of total explained variance (i.e., an increment in R² of only 0.0001; <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">Therneau & Atkinson, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Although this value seems very small, consider that the total effect for a continuous predictor (e.g., trial number) consists of multiple splits.
Each individual split might contribute a small proportion, but the total variance explained may still be substantial.
The minbucket and maxdepth arguments can be used to define the "largest meaningful tree" based on design considerations.
The minbucket argument specifies the minimum number of observations required in a final node.
We set minbucket = 106, which ensures that data from at least two consecutive trials for all 53 participants is segmented into one final node.
The maxdepth argument indicates the maximum number of splits allowed before reaching a final node, with a default setting of 30.
Determining sensible values for these stopping criteria can be challenging.
Alternatively, it is possible set cp = 0, minbucket = 1, and maxdepth = 30 to grow the full initial tree and determine the final tree by pruning alone.
Pruning is enabled by setting cv = TRUE.

The default option is no.SE = 1, pruning to the simplest tree with a cross-validation error within one standard error from the minimal cross-validation error (Breiman et al., 1984; Sela & Simonoff, 2012).
text.formatted: The default option is no.SE = 1, pruning to the simplest tree with a cross-validation error within one standard error from the minimal cross-validation error <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Breiman et al., 1984;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Sela & Simonoff, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: For our data, this setting resulted in overly simplistic trees that rarely detected time-varying or any experimental effects.
Therefore, we recommend pruning such that the complexity parameter with the minimal cross-validation error is used (no.SE = 0), as described in the introduction.
However, this recommendation may be specific to our data scenario, and further research on pruning recommendations for different data settings is needed.
Finally, another useful setting is to change the optimizer to "optim" using the lme.control argument, as the default "nlminb" often failed to converge in our pilot simulations.

text.text: This split shows that the tree models the previously observed slow decay in standard trials (see Figures 8 to 10) as a level change, demonstrating the tree's limitations in approximating smooth, especially quasilinear, functions.

At the bottom of the fit output, we find the covariance matrix of the random effects.
From this, we can calculate the random intercept SD = √ 1968 ms = 44 ms, the random slope SD = √ 171 ms = 13 ms, and the random effects correlation r = 249 44×13 = .44.
The interpretation of these random effects now concerns marginal effects, because the random effects structure is less complex than the fixed effects structure (no random trends and interaction).

Therefore, the random intercept variance quantifies the variation in participants' marginal standard trial RT and the random slope variance quantifies the variation in their marginal distraction effect.
RE-EM trees can also be expanded to include more complex, though only parametric, random-effects structures, such as individual linear or polynomial trends per experimental condition.
RE-EM trees can not model fully nonparametric individual trends because it is not possible to allow the tree structure to vary across participants.

Based on our simulation for random trends, we caution about using simple RE-EM trees as in Figure 12 when individuals vary substantially regarding trends and/or in situations with large number of trials.

text.text: This is a clear limitation of the RE-EM trees.
However, we also caution against including parametric random trends and interactions as a fix, because they severely complicate interpretation and the impact on model estimation remains unclear.

The only way to model different trees depending on person-characteristics in RE-EM trees is by including relevant person-level predictors for these subgroups as splitting variables, but research shows that RE-EM trees are not well suited for this purpose (Hany et al., 2026).

text.text: Researchers interested in detecting subgroups of participants with similar trends might instead want to consider different tree-based methods that are explicitly dedicated to detecting these subgroups (Abdolell et al., 2002; Eo & Cho, 2014; Fokkema et al., 2017; Kundu & Harezlak, 2019; Segal, 1992; Stegmann et al., 2018).

text.text: As a final caveat, we want to point out again that no inferential statistics or measures of uncertainty are included in the RE-EM tree output, even though the tree algorithm is associated with considerable uncertainty.
Trees produce largely different results for different samples, and their results also depend on random components, such as cross-validation, in the algorithm.
Some approaches to mitigate these issues are also applicable to repeated-measures data, for example, RE-EM ctrees (Fu & Simonoff, 2015) and mixed-effects random forests (Hajjem et al., 2014).

text.text: However, the latter can not be used with only two predictor variables.

Investigating time-varying experimental effects can elucidate underlying (cognitive) processes, increase statistical power, and avoid the risk of misleading comparisons of marginal effects across experiments of varying length.

Our simulations demonstrated that exact parametric models, lower order polynomial GCMs, and GAMMs can all effectively detect and model time-varying experimental effects across various trend shapes under realistic conditions provided an adequate random-effects structure.
Only for stepwise trends, RE-EM trees and GAMMs outperformed lower order polynomial GCMs.

For smooth trends, RE-EM trees showed no advantage over polynomial GCMs or GAMMs, as they also achieved a good approximation provided large numbers of trials and sample sizes, but showed worse generalization to new samples than the other models for small number of trials and participants and suffered from an increased FPR when random trends are not adequately modeled.
In the tutorial, we illustrated that, in practice, these models differ in flexibility, interpretability, statistical inference, and expandability to more complex fixed-and random-effects structures.
Ultimately, the selection of a model depends on the research goal.
If the goal is prediction, models from different classes can be compared using cross-validation, evaluating how accurately they predict observations that were not used for fitting.

For repeated-measures data, the validation scheme should reflect the intended prediction task: For example, assessing generalization to new participants requires holding out entire participants rather than individual observations (Rabinowicz & Rosset, 2022).
text.formatted: For repeated-measures data, the validation scheme should reflect the intended prediction task: For example, assessing generalization to new participants requires holding out entire participants rather than individual observations <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Rabinowicz & Rosset, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: With small samples, cross-validation estimates can be highly variable, so small differences in predictive performance should be interpreted cautiously (Varoquaux, 2018).
text.formatted: With small samples, cross-validation estimates can be highly variable, so small differences in predictive performance should be interpreted cautiously <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">(Varoquaux, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Information criteria such as AIC and BIC offer another approach to model comparison by balancing model fit against model complexity.

Both criteria have established asymptotic correspondences with specific cross-validation procedures for model selection, although the corresponding procedures and assumptions differ (Shao, 1997; Stone, 1977).
text.formatted: Both criteria have established asymptotic correspondences with specific cross-validation procedures for model selection, although the corresponding procedures and assumptions differ <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Shao, 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Stone, 1977)</ref>.

text.text: Comparisons require models fitted to the same observations and response scale using comparable likelihood definitions.
This is particularly important when comparing results across software packages, which may differ in the constants included in the reported log-likelihood and in how model complexity is counted.
Fitting the candidate models using the same software and estimation procedure, for example, fitting alternative GCMs in nlme, helps avoid these discrepancies (see Tutorial R Code).

Nevertheless, using the same software does not by itself guarantee comparability: Models with different fixed-effects structures should be compared using maximum likelihood rather than restricted maximum likelihood.

If the goal is to characterize the shape of a trend or a time-varying experimental effect, we recommend using the models together to assess which substantive conclusions depend on the modeling of time.
For example, agreement across models about an initial decline followed by a plateau provides stronger support for this qualitative pattern than its appearance in only one fitted curve.
Such comparisons can guide the development of a parametric model whose parameters have theoretical meaning, as is common in mathematical psychology.
A model developed through this exploratory process should subsequently be evaluated using independent data.
Balancing the strengths and weaknesses of each model, we propose the following workflow for investigating time-varying experimental effects (Figure 13).
text.formatted: Balancing the strengths and weaknesses of each model, we propose the following workflow for investigating time-varying experimental effects (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_21">13</ref>).

text.text: Most simple continuous trends can be reasonably approximated with polynomial models.

We recommend using lower order polynomials as the default modeling option due to their manageable parameter interpretation, availability of inferential statistics for parameters, as well as points of interest and ease of extension to model individual random trends.
Exact parametric models can be specified as MEMs when there is a specific assumption about the shape of the trend.
We recommend that they be used only when supported by strong theoretical grounds, as they can not capture deviating shapes and may obscure such shapes, potentially leading to false conclusions.

Because lower order polynomials, especially linear functions, are unable to depict more complex shapes (which are likely to occur in psychophysiological data) and are susceptible to artifacts at the edges of the data range (e.g., "wiggly" trends), we recommend complementing them with GAMMs.
If GAMM results are similar to GCM, the polynomial model is likely sufficiently complex.
Differences between GCMs and GAMMs at the edges of the data range may indicate artifacts in the GCM.
For more complex smooth trends, GAMMs should be preferred over higher order polynomials with many parameters.

Note that GAMMs without individual (random) trends can still be used to compare the shape of the spline to the polynomial curve visually, even though inference for the spline is not reliable when random trends are present.
RE-EM trees can be used to detect major deviations from proposed trends caused by abrupt level changes.

However, caution is advised when using RE-EM trees in small samples or with only a few trials due to their weak performance and instability under these circumstances, but also when substantial interindividual variation in trends was detected with the previous models.
At the current state of research on RE-EM trees, we recommend to only use them to complement results from other, more well established models.
Their use in any research project should be accompanied by appropriate critical reflection.

Regarding individual trends, we emphasize the existing recommendations to select an appropriate random effects structure to also investigate individual differences and to ensure correct statistical inference for the fixed effects estimates (Barr et al., 2013; Matuschek et al., 2017; Park et al., 2020), especially in experiments with many trials.

text.text: Finally, the initial theory on time-varying effects can be refined to incorporate explanations for the observed trends.
It is crucial to replicate findings in new samples to ensure robustness and generalizability.

The proposed workflow can be used to plan and preregister both a strategy for more exploratory (re-) analyses, with no or very limited prior knowledge about the time-varying effect, or more confirmatory analyses, when researchers want to test a specific shape or model class and only use GAMMs and/or RE-EM trees as robustness checks.

The linear B-spline basis function resembles overlapping triangular "hats".
At each knot, the corresponding function equals one, decreases linearly to zero at the neighboring knots, and remains zero outside that range (with the outer boundary being the range of the data).
Multiplying this function by a coefficient (weight) changes the height of the hat.
The fitted values are a weighted average of the basis functions of the nearest knots, as illustrated in Figure4a (e.g., De Boor, 1978).
Quadratic and cubic B-splines follow the same principle, but use smoother basis functions whose contributions overlap across more neighboring intervals (Figures4b and c).

The coefficients are estimated jointly, because the fit depends on their combined contributions.Selecting a high degree basis function and a large basis dimension k (number of basis functions, closely linked to the number of knots) makes the spline flexible but can also lead to overfitting.
